reference_opening.argument: This video is non-scam content because it discusses Fortnite V-Bucks gift cards for purchasing in-game currency, including price and denomination information. The creator-code overlay, requests for engagement, and item-shop promotion are described as ordinary audience engagement and commerce, without an associated payment requirement, investment return, or credential request.

citations.quote: New Fortnite V-bucks Gift Cards | New Way To Buy V-bucks
With these gift cards you can buy the same amount of vbucks as in game but without the need of a credit card.
these give you a 10 bucks gift card. thousand B bucks and Thirteen thousand five hundred B Bucks all for the prices of $10, $25 $40 and a hundred dollars
I would much rather prefer to go out and buy a gift card than have to put in my credit card information.

opening.argument: The presentation links access to the advertised digital asset with a concrete purchase decision and a separate creator-code action. Viewers are told that the cards make obtaining V-Bucks easier, then are directed toward the creator's code in the item shop. That combination turns an apparently informational announcement into a low-friction solicitation: acquire the asset, and support the promoter while doing so. The evidence does not establish that the cards are free, but it does show a direct action pathway for obtaining a game asset through a branded offer.

citations.quote: they have made it a lot easier now since they introduced these v bucks
remember to use code jellifoxy in the Fortnite item shop
With these gift cards you can buy the same amount of vbucks as in game but without the need of a credit card.

rebuttal.rebuttal: Calling the cards ordinary commerce does not answer the promotional linkage. The video does more than describe denominations: it emphasizes easier acquisition and ends by directing viewers to use the creator code. The absence of an explicit free reward or credential request does not eliminate a solicitation; it only narrows the kind of solicitation being made. The cited prices show a purchase mechanism, while the code shows how the promoter benefits from participation.

citations.quote: they have made it a lot easier now since they introduced these v bucks
remember to use code jellifoxy in the Fortnite item shop

true_side_reply.rebuttal: The argument identifies a purchase and a creator-code request, but neither is a low-barrier free-reward claim. The description expressly says the cards are a way to buy V-Bucks, and the cited code is a disclosed creator-support mechanism, not evidence that viewers must pay the creator or surrender information. The evidence therefore shows promotion of a conventional game purchase, not a deceptive acquisition flow.

opening.argument: Several risk signals appear together: a digital game asset, gift-card purchasing, an external social-media presence, and a creator code placed alongside the offer. The description supplies Twitch, Twitter, and Instagram destinations, while the video displays a prominent creator-code graphic. These elements create a funnel from attention to purchase and promoter support. The branded card artwork may make the offer look official, but the supplied material does not independently establish who fulfills the cards, how redemption works, or what protections a buyer has. A careful judge should treat the polished appearance and convenience framing as persuasion, not proof of safety.

Use Support-a-Creator code: "JELLYFOXY"

rebuttal.rebuttal: The defense treats recognizable product imagery and stated prices as resolving the risk, but those details establish only what is being promoted. They do not establish fulfillment, redemption safeguards, or that the surrounding links are irrelevant to the purchase decision. The external destinations and creator-code overlay are not incidental background: they are attached to the offer and amplify the route from viewer attention to transaction.

citations.quote: Use Support-a-Creator code: "JELLYFOXY"

true_side_reply.rebuttal: The risk list is being inflated beyond the evidence. The description identifies ordinary social channels and a Support-a-Creator code, while the frames show recognizable Fortnite V-Bucks cards with stated denominations. Nothing supplied shows an external claim or verification flow, a hidden fee, compromised credentials, or a false return. Missing proof of every possible safeguard is not proof that the ordinary purchase is deceptive.

opening.argument: Although framed as a quick heads-up about a new feature, the content functions as a sales pitch. The title calls it a “New Way To Buy” V-Bucks, the narration stresses that acquisition is easier, and the closing directs viewers to use the creator's code in the item shop. The description also presents the offer as newly available and supplies promotional channels. This is not a neutral explanation of game mechanics; it steers viewers toward buying a game asset and supporting the presenter, which is the relevant solicitation behavior.

A new way to buy v-bucks has been made available by Epic Games.

rebuttal.rebuttal: The defense's description of ordinary commerce concedes the central point: this content is steering viewers toward a purchase. Calling the steering “audience engagement” does not make it neutral, especially when the closing request names the promoter's code. The title and narration are structured around ease and availability, while the commercial call to action supplies the practical next step.

citations.quote: New Fortnite V-bucks Gift Cards | New Way To Buy V-bucks
remember to use code jellifoxy in the Fortnite item shop

true_side_reply.rebuttal: Promotion alone does not convert a legitimate product into a scam. The title and narration accurately describe buying V-Bucks gift cards, and the creator-code request is transparent rather than disguised. The evidence shows no promise of free assets, unusual returns, investment, or a deceptive claim pathway; it shows a creator discussing a purchasable game product and asking viewers to use a disclosed support code.
